title: Monthly, quarterly, year over year
prompt: `orders` has one row per non-cancelled order, with `order_date` and `revenue`. Build `monthly` (revenue per calendar month, month-end labels) and `monthly_orders` (number of orders per month) with `resample`. Build `quarterly` (revenue per quarter) and `yoy`, its growth versus the same quarter a year earlier as a fraction (1.0 means +100%). Finally set `best_weekday` to the name of the weekday with the highest total revenue.
hints: Put the dates in the index first: `by_time = orders.set_index("order_date")`, then `by_time.resample("ME")["revenue"].sum()`.
Count orders with `["order_id"].count()` (or `.size()`) on the same resampler. Quarters use `"QE"`.
`quarterly.pct_change(4)` compares with four quarters earlier. For the weekday: `orders.groupby(orders["order_date"].dt.day_name())["revenue"].sum().idxmax()`.
explanation: `resample` needs a datetime index, which `set_index("order_date")` provides; `"ME"` and `"QE"` label each bucket by its last day. November 2025 had 325 orders and 75,334 dollars of revenue. `pct_change(4)` on a quarterly series is the year-over-year view: the first four values are `NaN` because 2023 is not in the data, and Q4 2025 grew 179.5% on Q4 2024, in line with the 145-200% growth of the other 2025 quarters. Saturday brings in the most revenue, though the weekday differences are small compared with the seasonal ones.

checks.monthly: `monthly` has 24 months, with November 2025 at about 75,334
checks.yoy: `yoy` is 1.795 for Q4 2025 and empty for 2024
checks.weekday: `best_weekday` is the top weekday by revenue
